definition: The Google Books Ngram Viewer is an online search engine that charts the frequencies of any set of search strings using a yearly count of n-grams found in printed sources published between 1500 and 2022 in Google's text corpora in English, Chinese (simplified), French, German, Hebrew, Italian, Russian, or Spanish.
details: There are also some specialized English corpora, such as American English, British English, and English Fiction. The program can search for a word or a phrase. The n-grams are matched with the text within the selected corpus, and if found in 40 or more books, are then displayed as a graph. The program supports searches for parts of speech and wildcards. It is routinely used in research.

explainer.lead: Google Books Ngram Viewer turns millions of digitized books into line charts showing how often words and phrases appear over time. It makes long-term language and cultural trends easy to explore, although errors and biases in the underlying books mean the charts need careful interpretation.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a huge library where a computer counts how often a word appears in books from each year, then draws those counts as a line. You could compare “nursery school” and “kindergarten” to see how their use changed. The lines show patterns in these books, not necessarily what everyone was saying or thinking.
tiers.practitioner: Choose a corpus, such as English, British English, or English Fiction, then enter comma-separated words or phrases and inspect the yearly chart; part-of-speech and wildcard searches are also supported. Only n-grams found in at least 40 books are indexed. Treat results cautiously because OCR mistakes, incorrect dates and categories, changing corpus composition, and weak early data for some languages can create apparent trends.
tiers.paperLevel: For a search string s, the Viewer charts a yearly n-gram frequency derived from the selected Google Books corpus, with printed sources spanning 1500–2022 and matches requiring occurrence in at least 40 books. Its creators described high-volume analysis of digitized texts as “culturomics” in a Science paper released on December 16, 2010. The corpora contain OCR and metadata errors, sampling and genre biases, and limited metadata, so observed frequencies cannot be treated as direct measurements of general linguistic or cultural change.

explainer.example: Search the English corpus for “nursery school, kindergarten.” The Viewer treats “nursery school” as a 2-gram and returns separate lines for the two terms, provided each meets the 40-book threshold, allowing their yearly frequencies to be compared across the selected period.

explainer.intuition: Instead of reading centuries of books one by one, count a word or phrase year by year and draw the result as a line. Comparing several lines can reveal changes in how often expressions appear in the selected collection.
howItWorks: Enter words or phrases, separated by commas, and choose a language or specialized English corpus.
The Viewer matches each search string against n-grams in that corpus; “nursery school,” for example, is a bigram.
Matches are included only when the n-gram occurs in at least 40 books.
Yearly frequencies are returned as plotted lines, with optional part-of-speech and wildcard searches.
explainer.whyItMatters: Released on December 16, 2010, the Viewer opened quantitative exploration of a database initially containing 500 billion words from 5.2 million books. Although designed for scholars, it lets anyone with a computer examine historical word-use trends.
misconceptions: A rising line does not by itself prove a general cultural shift; corpus composition and other biases can produce the pattern.
The charts are not error-free transcripts of publishing history because OCR, dating, and categorization mistakes remain.
The Viewer does not index every match: an n-gram must appear in at least 40 books.
Reliability varies by period and language, so dates before 1800 and early Chinese data require particular caution.
